Series::gcd¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::gcd(const Series& other) const
Series& Series::gcd_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::gcd_(const Series& rhs) const

What It Does¶

gcd() compares two integer series element by element and returns the greatest common divisor of every aligned pair. It is a pairwise transform, not a reduction: a six-element receiver and a broadcastable three-element operand produce six answers rather than one divisor shared by the whole receiver.

For a pair (a, b), the result is the largest non-negative integer that divides both values without a remainder. This makes gcd() useful wherever integers encode compatible units: reducing fractions, finding an exact block size shared by several measurements, or normalizing integer ratios before comparison.

Conventions, matching std::gcd:

  • the result is always >= 0, regardless of the signs of the inputs

  • gcd(x, 0) == |x| and gcd(0, 0) == 0

This is an integer-only operation. A floating-point or complex input raises rather than silently truncating.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&): the second integer operand. Its shape is broadcast against the receiver using the ordinary trailing-dimension rules. The two integer dtypes are promoted before the result is returned.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A new series containing the non-negative pairwise divisors. Its shape is the broadcast shape and its dtype is the promoted integer dtype. gcd_() writes that result into the receiver without replacing its storage; consequently, the broadcast result must fit the receiver’s existing shape and dtype.

Raises if either operand is a floating-point or complex series.

Gradient¶

gcd() is a discrete integer operation and is not differentiable.

In-Place Form¶

gcd_() is the in-place sibling of gcd(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — gcd_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<std::int64_t>{12, 18}, {2});
auto y = pluss::make_series(std::vector<std::int64_t>{8, 24}, {2});

x.gcd_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 6]

Examples¶

Example 1. Signs are dropped; gcd(x, 0) is |x|.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({12, 18, 0, -15}).gcd(pluss::make_series({8, 24, 5, 9})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 6, 5, 3]

gcd(0, 5) = 5, and gcd(-15, 9) = 3 — the negative sign is discarded.

Example 2. Broadcasting a row across a matrix.

auto measurements = pluss::make_series({{-12, 18, 0}, {20, -27, 14}});
auto block_sizes = pluss::make_series({{8, 6, 5}});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, measurements.gcd(block_sizes));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 4 6 5 ⎤
⎣ 4 3 1 ⎦

The row-shaped block_sizes is reused for each row of measurements. Notice that signs never leak into the result and that gcd(0, 5) contributes 5. This shape-preserving, pairwise form is convenient when each column represents a different unit or sampling interval.

Example 3. A floating-point input raises.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({12.0}).gcd(pluss::make_series({8.0}));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

gcd: integer inputs required

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Integer inputs only. Convert a float series with to(ScalarType::Int64) first if truncation is what you actually want.

  • gcd() may expand either operand through broadcasting. gcd_() cannot grow or retype its receiver, so use the out-of-place form when the result shape or promoted dtype differs.

  • The result is never negative, even when both inputs are.

  • gcd(0, 0) is 0, not an error.

  • Not differentiable.

Summary¶

gcd(a, b) is the elementwise greatest common divisor:

  • non-negative result; gcd(x, 0) = |x|, gcd(0, 0) = 0

  • integer inputs only — a float operand raises

  • not differentiable

  • gcd_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::lcm: the least common multiple, |a * b| / gcd(a, b).

  • Series::factor: the prime factorization the GCD can be read off from.

  • Series::remainder: the modulo the Euclidean algorithm iterates.
